prompt: What is the core problem version control solves once more than one person works on the same codebase?
choices: Keeping a single canonical backup of the project in case a laptop is lost
Letting multiple people change the same files independently over time while preserving who changed what and why, and giving a way to reconcile conflicting changes
Making code run faster by tracking performance metrics across commits
Automatically formatting code consistently across contributors

prompt: In real day-to-day git use, why do experienced developers run `git status` far more often than beginners do?
choices: Git refuses to let you commit unless you've run git status first
It shows exactly what's staged, what's changed but unstaged, and what's untracked, so you always know what your next commit would actually contain
It automatically stages all modified files for you
It replaces the need for git log entirely

prompt: In one sitting you fixed a login bug, updated the README, and started a new settings screen. What's the best committing practice?
choices: Run git add . once and make a single commit describing all three changes
Make three separate commits, each staged and described for just one of the changes
Only commit the bug fix now; skip committing the other two changes until they're finished
Wait until the whole project is done, then make one commit covering everything
It only checks whether the remote has new commits, without changing your local files
It downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into your current local branch
It uploads your local commits to the remote repository
It deletes your local changes and replaces them with the remote's version

prompt: You committed a .env file containing a real API key before setting up .gitignore. You've since added .env to .gitignore. What else must you do?
choices: Nothing — adding it to .gitignore automatically removes it from git's history and tracking
Run git rm --cached .env and commit that change to stop tracking it going forward, and treat the leaked key as compromised
Delete the .git folder and run git init again
Rename the file so git no longer recognizes it

prompt: Which of these belongs in a genuinely useful README for a real project?
choices: A complete listing of every file in the repository
A one-line description of what the project does and why, plus concrete install and usage instructions someone unfamiliar with the project could follow
The full git commit history copy-pasted into the file
Nothing beyond the project name, since good code comments make a README redundant

prompt: git status tells you: "Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits." What does this mean, and what should you do?
choices: Your local repository is corrupted and needs to be re-cloned
A teammate pushed 2 commits you don't have locally yet; run git pull to bring your branch up to date before continuing
You have 2 uncommitted local changes that still need to be committed
You are 2 commits ahead of the remote and need to push
